messages.subject: Re: Fwd: [DIST-SAMP] Line transects and point counts
parts:
Martin, I don't think breaking recording up into 8 min units is the
solution. For one thing, you might compromise the line transect design,
ending up with shorter lines in areas of high bird density, and hence
bias. I think you should design both surveys (line transect and point
transect) optimally, but so that total time in the field is approximately
equal. You can also adjust your results, to estimate the precision from a
fixed time in the field. Separately, I'll e-mail you a draft paper that
does just this. (That paper also argues against point transect counts of
fixed time duration, and in favour of a snapshot approach, because the
former can be biased due to bird movement during the count.)

Note that the term 'point counts' usually refers to just that - counts of
numbers of birds from a point, with no adjustment for detectability.
We tend to use the term 'point transect' when detection distances are
estimated, to distinguish between the two types of survey.

You ask about quadrat counts vs strip transect sampling. In fact, strict
transect sampling is just a form of quadrat sampling. The size and shape
of the quadrats depends on what is practical, given size of study area,
whether habitat is open of closed, etc. You may need to do some
preliminary work to assess what works best. The danger in your context of
long, narrow quadrats (i.e. strip transects) is that the edge-to-area
ratio is high, so you might end up following quite a few birds whose nests
turn out to be outside the strip.

Steve Buckland

> > Good morning all
> >
> > My name is Martin Taylor and I am an MSc student at the Conservation Ecology
> > Research Unit at University of Pretoria, South Africa. An initial part of my
> > research is the evaluation of the bird assemblages of Maputland's
> > regenerating coastal forests using two distance methods (line transects and
> > point counts) and subsequently comparing the performance of the two methods.
> >
> > I have completed an initial field work period with my main field work period
> > being planned for January/February of 2005. During my initial field work
> > period I conducted point counts and line transects in a given habitat to
> > the point where the curve on a species accumulation curve had flattened
> > out - for example this would require 6 line transects and 18 point counts in
> > a certain habitat. A problem I have encountered is that the amount of effort
> > for a point count (8 mins) is different to that of a line transect (approx
> > 35 mins)making a comparison of community variables obtained from each sample
> > of each method (such as species richness) as well as the rate at which the
> > species accumulation curve flattens out incomparable. I aim to solve this
> > for the next phase of my field work by walking the transects as per usual
> > but timing 8 min intervals while walking so as to be able to compare those
> > "8 min segments" to the 8 mins taken to complete a point count. I would
> > appreciate it if anybody has any ideas on this approach/ or a better method
> > as to how to deal with this.
> >
> > In addition, I plan to sample nests within the coastal dune forests -
> > initial observations have pointed out that most nests are found following an
> > observation of bird activity rather than finding the actual nest itself.
> > Would a strip transect method work better than quadrats?
> >
> > Thanks alot
> >
